extracted.intended_audience: biomedical researchers, NIH R01 applicants, grant administrators, policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical analysis of the NIH peer-review scoring system for R01-equivalent applications (FY2010–2013), focusing on the five scored review criteria, Overall Impact score, discussion status, and their relationships to funding outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the five research review criteria used to assess an application's scientific and technical merit (listed as Significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as a 1–9 criterion score averaged across reviewers for an application. In multivariate models Significance was the second most important predictor of Overall Impact and funding (Impact-model coefficient ~3.4; Funding-model odds ratio ~2.1 per one-point improvement). Significance interacts positively with Approach: applications scoring well on both have better-than-expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the five research review criteria used to assess the qualifications and track record of the investigator(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored on the 1–9 scale and averaged across reviewers. Investigator(s) scores tended to be clustered in low (good) ranges (median ~2.0). In models Investigator(s) had a smaller effect on Overall Impact than Approach or Significance, but its association with funding odds increased after controlling for other application and applicant characteristics (Funding-model odds ratio rose to ~1.4 in sub-model B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the five research review criteria used to assess novelty and originality of the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as an averaged 1–9 criterion score. Innovation had a moderate relationship to Overall Impact and funding (Impact-model coefficient ~1.4; Funding-model odds ratio ~1.5 per one-point improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the five research review criteria used to assess the strategy, methodology, and analyses of the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–9 and averaged across reviewers. Approach showed the greatest variability and the strongest association with Overall Impact and funding: a one-point improvement in Approach was associated with ~7.6 point improvement in Overall Impact and an odds ratio of ~6.2 for funding in the criterion-only Funding model. Approach was the single most important predictor and also displayed a significant positive interaction with Significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the five research review criteria used to assess institutional and resource support for the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Averaged 1–9 score. Environment scores were typically excellent (median ~2.0) and had the weakest correlation with Overall Impact; in some models the Environment effect was small and counterintuitive (better Environment scores sometimes associated with worse Overall Impact/funding odds after controlling for other criteria), indicating that strong environment alone does not offset weaknesses in other criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional applicable criteria (human/animal subjects; renewal/revision/resubmission)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional review criteria that are considered when applicable, such as whether an application involves human or animal subjects or is a renewal, revision, or resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items are not part of the five core scored criteria but are considered in review when relevant and can affect review outcomes or eligibility (e.g., applications with unresolved human/animal subject concerns were precluded from funding and removed from funding-model analyses). Renewal/resubmission status is an important application characteristic associated with better Impact scores and higher funding odds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system and aggregation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative scoring introduced in FY2010: five criterion scores (1–9) and an Overall Impact score (10–90).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each reviewer assigns 1–9 scores for the five criteria; criterion scores for an application are calculated by averaging all individual reviewers' criterion scores. The final Overall Impact score for each discussed application is the mean of eligible reviewers' Impact scores multiplied by 10 (range 10 [high impact] to 90 [low impact]). Applications not discussed (ND) do not receive a final numerical Overall Impact score. For modeling, criterion coefficients were interpreted per one-point improvement (lower = better).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion status (Discussed vs Non-Discussed) and funding likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an application is discussed in the SRG meeting determines assignment of an Overall Impact score and strongly influences funding chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ND (not discussed) applications do not receive an Overall Impact score and had almost no chance of funding (only one ND funded in FY2010–2013). ND applications had worse mean criterion scores. Being discussed is therefore a crucial step for obtaining a numerical Overall Impact and a realistic chance of funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative predictive importance of criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical ranking of the five criteria by their association with Overall Impact and funding outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study's multivariate models the ranking (largest to smallest effect) was Approach >> Significance > Innovation > Investigator(s) > Environment. Sub-model A (criteria only) explained ~74.8% of variation in Overall Impact scores. The Funding-model odds ratios per one-point improvement (criterion-only model) were approximately: Approach 6.2, Significance 2.1, Innovation 1.5, Investigator(s) ~1.0, Environment ~0.9. There was a significant positive interaction between Approach and Significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review process structure and group effects
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH peer review is a two-stage process: first-level SRG scientific/technical review (study section) and second-level Advisory Council/IC-level assessment of relevance to IC priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications are reviewed by SRGs (study sections) comprised of non-federal scientists; SRGs assign criterion and Impact scores, while IC Advisory Councils assess program relevance and funding recommendations. Analyses controlled for clustering by SRG using hierarchical random effects; intraclass correlations indicated some between-SRG variation (e.g., 4.2% in Impact model, 17.8% in Funding model), so SRG and IC differences can affect outcomes and should be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation and multicollinearity of criterion scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The five criterion scores are moderately to strongly correlated with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly meritorious applications tend to score well on all criteria, producing correlations among criteria (e.g., Investigator(s) vs Environment up to ~0.75). Multicollinearity can inflate variance of coefficient estimates (VIF rule-of-thumb), but in this large dataset VIF for each criterion was ≤2.2, mitigating concerns. Analysts should nonetheless be aware that correlations among criteria make isolated interpretation of any single criterion's effect more difficult.
